Kalshi's Red Sox Marketing Deal Collides With Its Own Massachusetts Legal Fight

Published August 26, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Kalshi, the federally regulated prediction market operator, announced multi-year marketing partnerships with five Major League Baseball franchises on August 25 — the Boston Red Sox, Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Diego Padres, and San Francisco Giants. It's Kalshi's first wave of MLB team deals, and it lands the company advertising real estate at Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium at the same time it's fighting a Massachusetts injunction over the very sports contracts the sponsorships are meant to promote.

What the deals cover

The five-team package gives Kalshi in-stadium signage, LED board placements, social media integrations, radio spots, and fan activations across all five markets. In Boston specifically, that includes Fenway Park signage and airtime on Red Sox flagship station WEEI. In Los Angeles, Kalshi picked up naming rights to Dodger Stadium's Gold Glove Bar. Combined, the five clubs represent close to 17% of MLB and an estimated 60 to 65 million fans, and the announcement follows similar single-team prediction-market sponsorships this summer — Novig with the New York Mets in late July, and Polymarket with the New York Yankees in early August — as trading platforms race to attach themselves to baseball ahead of the postseason.

The Massachusetts complication

The Red Sox partnership is notable because Massachusetts obtained a preliminary injunction against Kalshi back in January, barring the company from offering sports-event prediction contracts to residents of the state — a dispute that is currently on appeal. A spokesman for the Massachusetts Gaming Commission reiterated the state's position that residents who want to bet on sports should use an operator licensed by the commission, rather than a federally regulated exchange operating outside the state's own gaming framework. The Red Sox, notably, already carry sponsorship deals with two commission-licensed operators, BetMGM and DraftKings, alongside the new Kalshi marketing arrangement.

Why it matters

The episode is a clean illustration of the jurisdictional fight playing out across the country: prediction market platforms like Kalshi argue their sports-linked contracts are federally regulated commodities products beyond state gambling authority, while state gaming regulators argue those same products are functionally sports bets that require a state license. A pro sports franchise signing a marketing deal with a platform simultaneously blocked from serving that team's home-state customers underscores how unsettled the legal question still is — and it's a dynamic worth watching as more leagues and teams weigh similar sponsorships heading into football season.
